content: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is influenced by several factors, including genetic predisposition, hormonal influences, environmental triggers, and infections. 1. Genetic Predisposition: Variations in HLA class polymorphism are associated with an increased risk of developing SLE. Mutations or deficiencies in complement genes also contribute to susceptibility. Female sex hormones, particularly elevated levels of estrogen and prolactin, are implicated in the higher prevalence of SLE among women. 2. Autoimmune Mechanisms: SLE is fundamentally an autoimmune disease, characterized by the immune system attacking the body’s own tissues. 3. Infections: Certain infections are known to trigger or exacerbate SLE, including: Parvovirus B19 Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) Trypanosomiasis Mycobacterial infections 4. Environmental Triggers: Exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light can induce or worsen systemic manifestations of SLE. 5. Drug-Induced Lupus: Certain medications can lead to a lupus-like syndrome, which mimics SLE but is typically reversible upon discontinuation of the offending drug. Diagnosis of SLE The diagnosis of SLE is guided by the Systemic Lupus International Collaboration Criteria (SLICC), which were introduced in 2012 to improve diagnostic sensitivity and address limitations of the older ACR criteria. The SLICC criteria allow for a more comprehensive and accurate classification of SLE. 1. Diagnostic Requirements: A diagnosis of SLE is established if the patient meets at least 4 out of 17 criteria, with at least 1 clinical criterion and 1 immunologic criterion. Alternatively, a diagnosis can be made if there is biopsy-proven lupus nephritis in the presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) or anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) antibodies. 2. Criteria Considerations: A criterion is considered positive if one or more of the observations listed under that criterion are present in the patient. Each criterion is counted only once, regardless of the number of observations that fulfill it. These diagnostic guidelines ensure a systematic and standardized approach to identifying SLE, improving both sensitivity and specificity in clinical practice.
